subject: Critical Thinking
title: Prospect Theory: How We Really Make Choices
description: One-minute skill: Prospect Theory: How We Really Make Choices.

hook.text: Would you prefer a guaranteed $500 or a 50% chance at $1,000? Most take the sure thing.

buildup.text: Prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky): people evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point, not in absolute terms.

discovery.text: Key insights: losses hurt 2x more than equal gains, and we overweight small probabilities.

twist.text: Risk preference flips: we're risk-averse for gains but risk-seeking for losses.

climax.text: Prospect theory won a Nobel Prize. It replaced the rational actor model with a realistic map of human decision-making.

punchline.text: We don't maximize value. We minimize regret.

quiz.question: What does prospect theory predict about gains vs. losses?
options: People are risk-averse for gains and risk-seeking for losses

details.summary: Prospect theory, developed by Kahneman and Tversky, shows that people evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point rather than in absolute terms. Losses loom larger than gains, and we are risk-seeking when facing losses but risk-averse when facing gains.
details.whyItMatters: Prospect theory explains irrational behaviors in finance, insurance, and gambling that standard economics cannot, revealing how real humans actually decide.
takeaways: People evaluate gains and losses relative to a reference point
Losses hurt about twice as much as equivalent gains please
Risk preferences reverse depending on whether outcomes are framed as gains or losses

faq.question: How does prospect theory differ from classical economic theory?
faq.answer: Classical theory assumes people maximize total wealth rationally. Prospect theory shows we evaluate changes from a reference point, are loss-averse, and distort probabilities. Real humans are systematic in their irrationality.

faq.question: What is the significance of the reference point in prospect theory?
faq.answer: The same outcome can feel like a gain or a loss depending on the reference point. An employee moved from a $100K to $90K salary suffers, while one moved from $70K to $90K celebrates, despite the same final amount.
